Content:

If the complex number [MATH: z] satisfies [MATH: \textrm{Re}(z) > 0,] then the gamma function can be defined as the improper integral

[MATH: \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt.]

  • Integral III does not match the definition. The integrand [MATH: \dfrac{e^t}{t^{1-z}}] is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Here, we'll prove the recursive formula for the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)]

Content:
The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: Γ(z + 1)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}t^{z}e^{− t}dt; = − t^{z}e^{− t}|_{0}^{∞} − ∫_{0}^{∞} − zt^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt; = lim_(t → ∞)(− (t^{z})/(e^{t})) − (− (t^{z})/(e^{t}))|_{t = 0} + ∫_{0}^{∞}zt^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt; = 0 − 0 + z∫_{0}^{∞}t^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt_(⏟)_(Γ(z)); = zΓ(z)]

Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

Content:
This relationship holds for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1.] Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)]

Content:
For any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1,] the above identity states the following:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)]

Content:
Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

Content:
[MATH: Γ(n + 1)|= nΓ(n); = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ Γ(n − 1)^(⏞)^(Γ(n)); = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ (n − 2) ⋅ Γ(n − 2)^(⏞)^(Γ(n − 1)); = …; = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ (n − 2) ⋅ … ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(n!) ⋅ Γ(1)]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1).]

Content:
To evaluate [MATH: \Gamma(1),] we can use the definition of the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n!]

Content:
Previously, we used the fact that [MATH: \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}.] To prove this, we can directly compute the value of [MATH: \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)] using the definition of the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t]

Content:
We simplify this integral using the substitution [MATH: t = u^2,] which implies [MATH: \text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u.] Also, note that [MATH: u \to 0^+] as [MATH: t \to 0^+] and [MATH: u \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] So, we have

Content:
[MATH: t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u.]

Content:
Thus, we get

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u.]

Content:
This is directly related to the well-known Gaussian integral:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \sqrt{\pi}]

Content:
Since the integrand [MATH: e^{-u^2}] is even (i.e., symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis), we have

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi}.]

Content:
Substituting this result back into our expression for the Gamma function, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi} = \sqrt{\pi}.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Proof of the Recursive Formula

Content:
Here, we'll prove the recursive formula for the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)]

Content:
The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: Γ(z + 1)|= ∫_{0}^{∞}t^{z}e^{− t}dt; = − t^{z}e^{− t}|_{0}^{∞} − ∫_{0}^{∞} − zt^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt; = lim_(t → ∞)(− (t^{z})/(e^{t})) − (− (t^{z})/(e^{t}))|_{t = 0} + ∫_{0}^{∞}zt^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt; = 0 − 0 + z∫_{0}^{∞}t^{z − 1}e^{− t}dt_(⏟)_(Γ(z)); = zΓ(z)]

Item 13 — Tutorial: Proving the Relationship Between the Gamma Function and the Factorial

Content:
Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n) = (n-1)!]

Content:
This relationship holds for any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1.] Now, let's prove it.

Content:
First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)]

Content:
For any natural number [MATH: n \geq 1,] the above identity states the following:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)]

Content:
Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

Content:
[MATH: Γ(n + 1)|= nΓ(n); = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ Γ(n − 1)^(⏞)^(Γ(n)); = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ (n − 2) ⋅ Γ(n − 2)^(⏞)^(Γ(n − 1)); = …; = n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ (n − 2) ⋅ … ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(n!) ⋅ Γ(1)]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1).]

Content:
To evaluate [MATH: \Gamma(1),] we can use the definition of the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma(n+1) = n!]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Evaluating the Gamma Function at One-Half

Content:
Previously, we used the fact that [MATH: \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}.] To prove this, we can directly compute the value of [MATH: \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)] using the definition of the gamma function:

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t]

Content:
We simplify this integral using the substitution [MATH: t = u^2,] which implies [MATH: \text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u.] Also, note that [MATH: u \to 0^+] as [MATH: t \to 0^+] and [MATH: u \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty.] So, we have

Content:
[MATH: t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u.]

Content:
Thus, we get

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u.]

Content:
This is directly related to the well-known Gaussian integral:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \sqrt{\pi}]

Content:
Since the integrand [MATH: e^{-u^2}] is even (i.e., symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis), we have

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi}.]

Content:
Substituting this result back into our expression for the Gamma function, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi} = \sqrt{\pi}.]
